overview: Iluka Resources is an Australian critical minerals company with over 70 years of history as a leading global producer of zircon and high-grade titanium dioxide feedstocks (rutile and synthetic rutile) from mineral sands. The company is transforming into a diversified critical minerals producer by building Australia's first fully integrated rare earths refinery at Eneabba, Western Australia, targeted for commissioning in 2027, funded substantially by a non-recourse Australian government loan. Iluka's mining and processing operations are located exclusively in Australia (Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, Victoria), supported by a global marketing and distribution network across Asia, Europe and the Americas, and it also holds a 20% stake in ASX-listed Deterra Royalties.

business_model.summary: Iluka earns revenue selling mineral sands products (zircon, rutile, synthetic rutile, ilmenite) into global industrial end markets (ceramics, pigments, foundry, zirconium chemicals), priced mostly in USD and sold under a mix of spot and contracted/take-or-pay arrangements. It is building a second, higher-value business refining separated rare earth oxides (neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium) at Eneabba, which will generate revenue from 2027/2028 under long-term offtake contracts (e.g. a 2028-starting take-or-pay deal with a global automotive company for 1,200t/yr of magnet rare earth oxides). It also receives a dividend stream (100% passed through) from its 20% equity stake in Deterra Royalties, an iron-ore royalty company.

revenue_streams.name: Synthetic rutile / natural rutile (titanium feedstocks)
revenue_streams.trend: declining (idled capacity amid weak pigment demand)

revenue_streams.name: Ilmenite and other by-products (activated carbon, gypsum, iron concentrate)

business_model.customer_type: B2B industrial — pigment producers, ceramics/foundry manufacturers, zirconium chemical companies, and (for rare earths) automotive/magnet/defence manufacturers
business_model.geographic_mix: Production 100% Australia; mineral sands sales by region approx: China region 44-45%, Europe/Middle East/Africa/India ~27-32%, Other Asia/Rest of Asia ~11-18%, Americas ~7-10%, Japan ~1%

main_competitors: China Northern Rare Earth / state-owned Chinese rare earths producers
competitive_position.market_position: One of the world's largest producers of zircon and a leading producer of high-grade titanium dioxide feedstocks (synthetic rutile); an emerging, not-yet-operating entrant in separated rare earth oxides via Eneabba, positioned as a potential material Western (non-China) supplier with differentiated heavy rare earth (dysprosium/terbium) capability

moat_factors.description: Long-life, high-grade Australian ore bodies (Jacinth-Ambrosia, Balranald) and decades of mineral sands expertise across exploration, mining, processing and marketing
Eneabba refinery backed by a non-recourse A$1.65bn Export Finance Australia loan, reflecting Western governments' strategic push to build non-China rare earths supply chains
Eneabba designed to process diverse feedstocks from Iluka's own operations plus third-party agreements (Northern Minerals, Lindian Resources, VHM), reducing single-deposit dependence

moat_factors.factor: Diversified product/customer base and marketing network
moat_factors.description: Global marketing and distribution network and a differentiated full-suite (light and heavy) magnet oxide offering among Western rare earths suppliers
Management highlights achieving materially stronger zircon pricing than competitors despite weak markets, reflecting customer relationships and supply discipline

weaknesses: Mineral sands business is a commodity, cyclical price-taker exposed to Chinese competitor discounting and pigment-industry demand swings
Single-country production base (100% Australia) concentrates operational, cost and regulatory risk
Rare earths business is pre-revenue, capital-intensive, and dependent on execution of a complex, delayed (2026→2027) refinery build
High and rising net debt (Group net debt ~$1.15bn at H1 2026) driven by simultaneous mineral sands downturn and rare earths capex
Dependence on government financing (EFA loan) and offtake conditions creates execution/political risk

growth_drivers: Eneabba rare earths refinery commissioning (targeted 2027) creating a new, higher-margin revenue stream in light and heavy magnet rare earth oxides

Secular/geopolitical tailwind: Western governments and manufacturers seeking to de-risk rare earths supply chains away from China (export restrictions in 2025, US government-MP Materials price floor, growing EV/defence/wind demand for NdPrDyTb)

Ramp-up of Balranald mine (NSW) — a high-grade, novel underground mining project reaching commissioning/production in 2026, diversifying the mineral sands production base and adding rare earth credits
Wimmera project (Victoria) definitive feasibility study, a potential multi-decade source of light and heavy rare earths and zircon, due for Board consideration in H1 2027
Third-party feedstock agreements (Northern Minerals, Lindian Resources, VHM Limited) extending refinery feedstock optionality and life
Potential downstream move into rare earth metallisation (metal, not just oxide) — feasibility study concluding in 2026
Restart optionality on idled Cataby mine and SR2 synthetic rutile kiln once mineral sands market conditions and pricing improve
20% Deterra Royalties stake providing a steady, low-risk dividend stream to help fund the rare earths build

business.description: Subdued pigment/titanium dioxide demand, competitor price discounting (notably Chinese zircon producers) and customer financial distress (e.g. Venator administration) have depressed prices and volumes, forcing production curtailments at Cataby and SR2
Key synthetic rutile offtake customers have entered administration/restructuring (Venator); Rio Tinto's strategic review of its RTIT titanium dioxide business could reshape industry structure

Refinery commissioning has already slipped from 2026 to 2027; construction ~60-65% complete with remaining structural/mechanical/piping work and ramp-up risk; capital estimate of $1.7-1.8bn could still move
Novel underground mining technology; commissioning took longer than planned in 2026 due to stope-void preservation and pipe-connection issues

financial.description: Group net debt grew to ~$1.15bn by H1 2026 (mineral sands $273m + rare earths $877m), with mineral sands free cash flow negative for several periods amid the downturn

financial.risk: USD revenue / AUD cost currency mismatch
financial.description: Revenue is predominantly USD-denominated while costs are largely AUD; AUD appreciation in H1 2026 (70.2c vs 66.0c) was a material earnings headwind; the Group partially hedges
FY2025 net loss of $288m included $351m of asset impairments and $216m of inventory net-realisable-value write-downs amid weak markets
Dividend framework pays out 100% of Deterra dividends plus a minimum 40% of mineral sands free cash flow; mineral sands FCF has been negative in recent halves, pressuring the policy

regulatory.description: Access to the full A$1.65bn EFA facility was conditional on securing qualifying offtake agreements; future drawdowns and loan terms remain subject to government/EFA requirements
Ongoing legacy rehabilitation liabilities in Australia and the United States (e.g. former Old Hickory/Concord mine in Virginia) carry long-dated environmental and closure obligations
US tariffs on Chinese pigment imports and broader trade tensions have disrupted the titanium dioxide pigment industry, Iluka's key end customer base

macro.description: China's 2025 export restrictions on rare earths (partly in response to US tariffs) are a double-edged factor: they validate Iluka's strategic rationale but also signal the volatility and geopolitical risk inherent in the sector Iluka is entering

~90% of titanium dioxide feedstock demand serves the pigment/paint industry, heavily tied to construction activity; a prolonged soft US/global housing market has weighed on Iluka's titanium feedstock sales

macro.risk: Commodity price benchmarks and manipulation risk
macro.description: Management has flagged the risk of price manipulation in rare earths markets and the importance of benchmarks grounded in commercial fundamentals rather than geopolitically distorted indices (e.g. Asian Metal Index)
Middle East conflict-related energy supply disruptions raised input costs and unit cash costs in H1 2026

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Mineral sands (zircon/titanium feedstocks) is in a cyclical downturn with oversupply and weak pigment-industry demand, though supply discipline and depleting high-grade deposits support a longer-term structural case; rare earths has a strong secular growth outlook driven by EVs, wind turbines, robotics, defence and Western supply-chain diversification away from China
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — mineral sands revenue and margins are strongly cyclical, tied to global construction, pigment production economics and competitor supply discipline; rare earths will add a structurally growing but currently pre-revenue segment
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-high — rising net debt (~$1.15bn) and ongoing large capital program (Eneabba, Balranald, Wimmera) make financing costs and bank facility (MOFA) terms increasingly relevant to earnings and cash flow
key_input_costs: Labour and contractor costs for Eneabba/Balranald construction

recent_developments.event: September quarter production report: Z/R/SR production ~76kt (up from ~58kt in Q2); mineral sands revenue ~$219m, down ~7% YoY; Eneabba refinery reported ~65% complete, capex to date ~A$1.237bn

Canaccord Genuity maintained Buy rating but cut price target to A$6.90 from A$7.25 following the September quarter, citing mineral sands as a drag on the more attractive rare earths business and flagging Eneabba commissioning as the key de-risking catalyst

Reported a net loss after tax of $24m for H1 2026 (vs $92m profit in H1 2025); revenue down 21% to $455.9m; underlying mineral sands EBITDA fell 81% to $41m; interim dividend of 3 cents/share declared

Executed first binding rare earths offtake agreement — a multi-year take-or-pay contract with a global automotive company for 1,200t/yr of magnet rare earth oxides, commencing 2028; this satisfied the offtake condition allowing Export Finance Australia to confirm full access to the A$1.65bn non-recourse loan; Civmec awarded the remaining structural/mechanical/piping/electrical/instrumentation (SMPEI) contract at Eneabba

Balranald mine (NSW) commenced mining and produced heavy mineral concentrate for the first time; commissioning took longer than planned due to stope-void preservation and mining-pipe connection issues, since addressed
Agreement concluded with VHM Limited (ASX:VHM) for rare earths concentrate feedstock supply to Eneabba, adding to existing agreements with Northern Minerals and Lindian Resources

FY2025 net loss of $288m (post $351m impairment and $216m inventory write-down); underlying mineral sands EBITDA of $300m (margin 31%, down from 42%); production suspended at Cataby mine and the SR2 synthetic rutile kiln from 1 December 2025 due to weak demand; zircon sales relatively resilient despite competitor price discounting

Rio Tinto initiated a strategic review of its RTIT titanium dioxide business (the world's largest merchant producer of titanium dioxide feedstocks), a development management says is likely to have lasting consequences for the mineral sands industry
Board changes: G Meyerowitz appointed director 1 April 2026; L Saint resigned 30 April 2026

guidance.management_commentary: Chair James Mactier and CEO Tom O'Leary describe 2025-2026 as 'a tale of two businesses' — mineral sands weighed down by cyclically weak pigment demand while rare earths has been validated by geopolitical supply-chain disruption and government support. Management emphasises operational discipline (curtailing Cataby/SR2), a strong inventory buffer (>$1bn), and confidence that Iluka is 'well positioned to respond when demand conditions improve.' On rare earths, management stresses disciplined execution at Eneabba, prioritising binding offtake agreements that balance customer supply security with fair value and protection against price manipulation, and highlights Iluka's differentiated full-suite (light and heavy) magnet oxide capability relative to other Western suppliers.

bull_case: Eneabba refinery positions Iluka as one of very few non-China, government-backed, vertically integrated separated rare earth oxide producers at a time of intense Western strategic interest and supply-chain de-risking
Differentiated heavy rare earth (dysprosium/terbium) capability is rare among Western suppliers and could command premium, government-supported pricing (cf. US MP Materials price floor precedent)
Substantial government financing (A$1.65bn non-recourse EFA loan) de-risks the capital structure for the rare earths build without diluting equity holders as heavily as a market raise would

Mineral sands business retains a large inventory buffer (>$1bn), diversified product mix, cost discipline and an all-Australian low-geopolitical-risk operating base, positioning it to benefit from any cyclical recovery in zircon/titanium feedstock demand

New growth optionality from Balranald (high-grade, now in production), Wimmera (DFS due H1 2027) and third-party feedstock agreements (Northern Minerals, Lindian, VHM) extends the resource pipeline for decades
bear_case: Mineral sands markets remain deeply cyclical and weak, with Chinese competitor discounting, pigment-customer distress (Venator) and a major competitor (Rio Tinto RTIT) strategic review creating industry structure uncertainty
Eneabba has already slipped from 2026 to 2027 commissioning and remains a large, complex, first-of-kind construction project with ongoing execution risk and capital cost exposure ($1.7-1.8bn)

Group net debt has risen sharply (~$1.15bn at H1 2026) while the core mineral sands business generates negative free cash flow, raising financing and dividend-sustainability concerns until Eneabba generates revenue

Rare earths revenue is still 1-2+ years away (first offtake starts 2028) — the stock is being asked to fund a pre-revenue, capital-intensive project through a severe cyclical trough in its legacy business

AUD appreciation against the predominantly USD-denominated revenue base is a direct earnings headwind, and broader geopolitical/trade volatility (tariffs, China export policy) adds unpredictability to both segments
